articles.title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
articles.summary: The Amazon rainforest is a crucial buffer against climate change - but deforestation had expanded under former president Jair Bolsonaro.
articles.content:
Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off in which the rainforest's future is a key issue.

Left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.

Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off on 25 October, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.

Satellite data shows that in the year to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%.

The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and measurable reduction in deforestation rates in the Amazon rainforest and Brazil's savanna, which has broad environmental significance given the Amazon's crucial role in climate regulation. The story highlights a clear positive impact on conservation efforts with detailed data on the decline, reflecting meaningful progress in climate action.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Brazil’s Amazon has seen its biggest drop in deforestation ever, signaling progress in protecting the rainforest just before a key election.

articles.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.
articles.content:
Plastic pollution is one of the world's most persistent environmental problems. Vast amounts of discarded plastic accumulate in the oceans, sometimes forming enormous garbage patches that threaten marine life. Most conventional plastics break down extremely slowly because microorganisms struggle to digest the synthetic polymers from which they are made. Instead of disappearing, these materials gradually fragment into increasingly smaller particles, including microplastics and nanoplastics.

Yet plastic waste is not completely beyond the reach of nature. Bacteria and other microorganisms can colonize its surfaces, forming communities known as biofilms. These communities create a distinctive microbial ecosystem that scientists call the "plastisphere."

Researchers at the University of Konstanz have now discovered an unusual enzyme that could reveal how some bacteria are becoming better equipped to break down certain types of plastic. The enzyme can digest particular polyesters and biodegradable plastics, but it has another unexpected ability: it can also break down penicillin, suggesting a possible connection to antibiotic resistance.

Scientists have nicknamed it the "Pac-Man enzyme" because its molecular structure features a remarkably wide opening where chemical reactions take place, known as the active site. The discovery suggests that bacteria may be adapting to digest certain plastic materials more quickly than researchers previously believed.

However, the findings also highlight an important limitation. For microorganisms to make a meaningful difference in reducing plastic pollution, more plastic products would need to be made from biodegradable materials that contain chemical bonds microbes can break apart.

Testing How Bacteria Break Down Bioplastics

To investigate how microorganisms digest biodegradable plastics, University of Konstanz biologists Harry Lerner and David Schleheck studied the entire process of microbial decomposition. They wanted to determine not only whether the materials could be completely broken down, but also which microorganisms were responsible and what biological mechanisms allowed them to do it.

The researchers examined the composition of the microbial communities involved and analyzed their collective genetic information (the metagenome). This approach allowed them to search for genes that might produce enzymes capable of breaking apart plastic polymers.

Their experiments focused on long-chain aliphatic polyesters (LCAP), a class of biodegradable plastic materials developed by a research team led by chemist Stefan Mecking. These materials contain chemical bonds that certain microorganisms can potentially break down, unlike the more resistant structures found in many conventional plastics.

The collaborative findings were published in The ISME Journal.

To observe how the bioplastics behaved in a natural environment, the team placed samples beneath the surface of forest soil at the university's botanical garden.

"We buried small pieces of LCAP bioplastic film in the upper humus layer in the forest at the university's botanical garden, about ten centimeters deep," explains Harry Lerner.

"This layer is where the breakdown of cellulose and other natural polymers, such as cutin - a plant-based polyester - takes place."

Humus is the upper layer of soil rich in decomposing organic matter, where microorganisms play a major role in recycling nutrients. Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls, while cutin is a naturally occurring polyester that helps form the protective outer covering of plants.

The researchers selected this environment because its microorganisms already possess the biological machinery needed to break down complex natural materials.

Bioplastics Disappeared Within About a Year

Alongside the outdoor experiment, the scientists carried out laboratory tests using soil collected from the same forest. They mixed powdered bioplastics into the soil and monitored microbial activity over the course of an entire year.

One important measurement was the amount of carbon dioxide, or CO2, released from the samples. As microorganisms consume and metabolize organic materials, they produce carbon dioxide through respiration. Tracking this gas helped the researchers determine how actively the microbes were breaking down the plastics.

The buried plastic films remained in the forest soil for a full year, allowing the team to compare decomposition under natural conditions with the carefully monitored laboratory experiments.

To assess the results, the scientists also tested cellulose, other biodegradable plastics, conventional polyethylene plastic, and soil samples without added materials.

"Cellulose, other types of bioplastics such as PHBV and PCL, as well as high-density plastic (HDPE) and untreated soil were used as controls in the laboratory. We found that all bioplastic materials were completely degraded within roughly 250 to 330 days. Cellulose broke down after about 80 days, whereas virtually no degradation occurred for HDPE," says Lerner.

The difference was striking. While the biodegradable plastics were completely broken down within approximately nine to eleven months, conventional high-density polyethylene showed almost no decomposition.

These results demonstrate why the chemical makeup of plastic matters so much. Some polymers contain bonds that microbial enzymes can attack, allowing bacteria to dismantle them into smaller molecules. Others, including widely used polyethylene, are far more resistant to biological degradation.

Mysterious Holes Reveal How Bacteria Eat Plastic

When the researchers recovered the plastic films from the forest soil, they discovered something unexpected.

Using electron microscopy, which can reveal structures far too small to see with an ordinary light microscope, the team examined the surfaces of the buried materials. They found numerous tiny holes, each approximately matching the dimensions and shape of an individual bacterial cell.

The unusual pattern suggested that bacteria were doing more than simply attaching themselves to the plastic. They appeared to be breaking into the material itself.

"We hypothesized that bacteria are coated with plastic-depolymerases anchored to their cell surfaces. This would enable them to digest their way into the material and become embedded within the film, leaving behind microscopic holes of exactly this type," explains Lerner.

Depolymerases are enzymes that break large molecules called polymers into smaller chemical units. If these enzymes are attached directly to the outside of a bacterium, they could allow the microorganism to digest the surrounding material while remaining in close contact with it.

This would help explain the microscopic cavities observed in the plastic films. Rather than relying entirely on enzymes released into the environment, the bacteria might be able to break down the material directly at their surfaces.

Scientists Identify the Plastic-Eating "Pac-Man Enzyme"

To find the biological machinery behind this unusual behavior, Lerner extracted DNA from the entire community of microorganisms living in the soil samples.

He then sequenced the genetic material and carefully analyzed the extensive data to determine which microbes and genes became especially abundant as the bioplastics decomposed.

One gene stood out. It was strongly enriched specifically in forest soil containing LCAP, suggesting that it could play an important role in breaking down the biodegradable polyester.

Further analysis revealed that the gene produces an esterase, a type of enzyme capable of splitting certain chemical bonds found in esters. These bonds are present in many naturally occurring substances as well as in various biodegradable polyesters.

What made this particular enzyme especially interesting was how it was positioned on bacterial cells.

Its genetic instructions included a secretion signal that directs the enzyme outside the cell, along with a lipid anchor that holds it firmly to the cell membrane.

This arrangement means the enzyme can remain attached to the bacterium's surface while attacking nearby plastic molecules. Its unusually exposed active site also provides space for the enzyme to interact with polymer chains.

The researchers had identified the molecular mechanism they were looking for, along with the enzyme they named "Pac-Man."

A Surprising Connection to Antibiotic Resistance

The discovery became even more intriguing when scientists examined the enzyme's molecular structure.

Although it resembled esterases, which are known for breaking down ester bonds, it also shared structural similarities with another important family of bacterial enzymes: beta-lactamases.

These enzymes are well known for their role in antibiotic resistance. Some bacteria produce beta-lactamases that disable antibiotics such as penicillin by breaking open a critical part of their chemical structure, known as the beta-lactam ring.

"Its structure resembles that of esterases, but also that of beta-lactamases, which are bacterial enzymes that are capable of cleaving the beta-lactam ring of certain antibiotics, such as penicillin, thereby making bacteria resistant to antibiotics," says Lerner.

Laboratory experiments confirmed that the newly discovered enzyme was capable of performing both types of chemical reactions.

It could break polyester chains into their individual building blocks, known as monomers, while also cleaving penicillin.

This dual activity was particularly surprising because plastic degradation and antibiotic breakdown are usually considered separate biological functions.

The finding raises the possibility that some enzymes involved in plastic decomposition could also contribute to antibiotic resistance. However, demonstrating that an enzyme can chemically break down penicillin in the laboratory does not establish that it provides antibiotic resistance to living bacteria.

Could Plastic-Eating Bacteria Help Solve Plastic Pollution?

The discovery also raises a broader question about how rapidly microorganisms can adapt to synthetic materials introduced into their environment.

For most of Earth's history, plastic pollution did not exist. Microorganisms evolved enzymes to digest naturally occurring substances, including plant fibers and other complex organic molecules.

Modern plastics have introduced an enormous new collection of potential carbon sources into the environment, but many of these materials remain chemically inaccessible to microbes.

"The plastisphere is a new habitat in our environment," explains Schleheck.

"Humans have only been introducing plastic into the environment in significant quantities for around 50 to 75 years. Since then, it has theoretically been available to microbial communities - such as bacteria, yeasts and fungi - as an additional source of carbon and energy for their growth. By 'theoretically', I mean that they would certainly like to use the plastic as a growth substrate - but they cannot, because the materials are actually indigestible to microbial metabolism and are therefore hardly degraded."

The Pac-Man enzyme suggests that this barrier may not be absolute for every type of plastic.

Some bacteria appear capable of using specialized enzymes to attack biodegradable polyesters, potentially allowing them to exploit these materials as sources of energy and nutrients.

For scientists studying plastic pollution, the finding offers a promising clue about how biological degradation might be improved. It also suggests that microbial communities could be adapting to certain synthetic polymers more rapidly than previously anticipated.

However, the results do not mean that bacteria are suddenly capable of consuming the enormous amounts of conventional plastic already accumulating in the environment. The experiments showed that polyethylene remained largely unaffected, even as the biodegradable plastics decomposed.

Instead, the researchers emphasize the importance of designing materials that microorganisms can actually digest.

"I find this encouraging, because it seems that bacteria can adapt to breaking down polyester plastics more quickly than we expected. To tackle the environmental problem of plastic pollution, we humans need to work with the capabilities of microbes. Ideally, this would involve using only polymers with biochemical breaking points, such as the hydrolysable ester bonds in polyesters like LCAP or other types of bioplastics," concludes Schleheck.

The discovery offers a glimpse of a potentially more sustainable approach to plastic production. Rather than expecting microorganisms to break down materials that are naturally resistant to decomposition, scientists could develop plastics with chemical structures that make biological recycling possible.

The Pac-Man enzyme illustrates how bacteria can exploit these molecular weak points, offering new insight into the relationship between plastic pollution, microbial adaptation, and the future of biodegradable materials.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery of a plastic-degrading enzyme that could help address the global problem of plastic pollution. The discovery has broad environmental implications by revealing microbial mechanisms that can break down biodegradable plastics in natural soil within about a year, contrasting with the persistence of conventional plastics. The research is detailed, focused on a single topic, and provides meaningful insights into microbial adaptation and sustainable plastic design, offering hope for improved plastic waste management and environmental conservation.

articles.title: Daily briefing: Bleached corals revived by healthy neighbour’s touch
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03336-0Ghostly white corals are fully restored in eight weeks by contact with a healthy counterpart. Plus, arXiv is capping submissions per researcher and four good news stories to brighten your day.
articles.content:
Ghostly white corals are fully restored in eight weeks by contact with a healthy counterpart. Plus, arXiv is capping submissions per researcher and four good news stories to brighten your day.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

In stressful conditions, corals expel the symbiotic algae that give them their colour from their tissues. Putting a bleached coral in contact with a healthy one (left) can restore it to full health within eight weeks (right).Credit: Danny Collins

Scientists have successfully restored bleached coral in the lab by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment. Researchers found that when a healthy piece of Pocillopora damicornis coral rested against a bleached piece, the two fused together to create a bridge across which algal symbionts can spread. This transfer fully restored the bleached coral within eight weeks, even if the healthy piece was removed after a week. The result “can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable” to reverse widespread coral decline, says marine ecologist and study co-author Fiorenza Micheli.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Science Advances paper

The preprint server arXiv has introduced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher in a bid to clampdown on a deluge of submissions, many generated by artificial intelligence. The limit is the latest measure to prevent its voluntary moderators from being overwhelmed by submissions, says astrophysicist Steinn Sigurðsson, scientific director of arXiv. Some researchers support the cap; others counter that it doesn’t solve the root problem. AI slop will “simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem”, says Natalie Khalil, the founder of AI-assisted peer-review platform Reviewer3.

Nature | 5 min read

A study of more than 100,000 people has revealed some surprising benefits of brown fat — a type that burns calories to generate heat. Researchers found that people with ‘active’ brown fat are less affected by health issues — such as type 2 diabetes, depression and anxiety — than those without it. The risk of these conditions decreased the more active brown fat a person had. The study is retrospective, so can’t confirm that brown fat is causing these benefits, but “it’s still a very interesting and surprising study”, says molecular biologist Irfan Lodhi.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Nature paper

When presented with two shapes, one with spikes and one rounded, and asked to designate them ‘bouba’ and ‘kiki’, people tend to agree that kiki is the spiky one — and so do dogs. Researchers found that when presented with images of these shapes, domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) more often looked at and moved toward the round shape when the word ‘bouba’ was played from a speaker, and vice versa. The results could suggest that dogs make similar connections between visual information and sounds to humans.

ScienceAlert | 5 min read

Reference: Proceedings of the Royal Society B paper

Features & opinion

Nature’s latest collection of stories selected to bring readers joy includes the newest penguin species described by science, and news that the island nation of Mauritius has become the first country in the world to reduce its number of people with type 2 diabetes — an impressive feat with diabetes rates rising globally, researchers say.

Nature | 5 min read

A technique called metagenomic testing can screen for every microorganism that might be present in a sample, rather than searching for one in particular. Now hospitals are trialling ways of using these tests to quickly identify whether acute illnesses that cause neurological symptoms are bacterial, viral or autoimmune in origin to inform more effective treatment. Interpreting the results of metagenomic tests — which pick up pathogens, harmless microbes and contamination alike — can be a rate-limiting step, but advances in AI have enabled a faster sort of useful data from noise.

BBC Future | 6 min read

The US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has updated On Being a Scientist, its bible for graduate students and early career researchers first published in 1989. Things have changed since the last edition, in 2009, note engineer Mitul Luhar, chemist and dean Emily Pentzer and psychologist Alan Leshner, who was formerly head of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. “Shifts in research priorities and funding place new expectations and pressures on scientists,” they write. “Early-career researchers feel the consequences most acutely.”

Issues in Science and Technology | 9 min read

Reference: On Being a Scientist: A Guide to the Responsible and Ethical Conduct of Research

This has broad implications for coral reef conservation and ecosystem recovery, offering a potentially scalable solution to reverse widespread coral decline. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a positive environmental impact with wide significance.

articles.title: What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees
articles.summary:

The post What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Every fall there’s a pull to tidy things up. Cut back the perennials, rake the leaves, clear the beds, put the garden to rest. It feels satisfying, honestly, and spring does seem to start from a cleaner place. The thing is, all that leaf litter, those hollow stems, those patches of scraggly dead plant matter? That’s where the bees are.

Over 3,600 bee species are native to the United States, and most of them are not honey bees. It’s the native wild bees, including mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, long-horned bees, bumble bees, and hundreds of others, that are in steep decline. Most are solitary: each female builds her own nest, lays her eggs, stocks them with food, seals them up, and dies. As Matthew Shepherd, Director of Outreach and Education at the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, explains, the offspring “complete most of their life stages in the cell, remaining there until the following year, when they emerge at the same season their mother was active.” That nest is almost certainly somewhere in your garden.

Sam Droege, Wildlife Biologist at the USGS, says wild bees are nesting above ground and in the ground somewhere nearby no matter where you live. Ecological landscape designer Kim Eierman puts it plainly: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.”

Most of what they need is already there, and the beauty of this solution is that all you have to do is less.

What to do with the fallen leaves

Move them rather than bag them. Bumble bee queens hibernate by digging a few inches underground or into leaf mulch, so piling leaves onto flower beds or into a back corner of the yard makes them a winter home. Leaf piles also give fireflies and other small garden creatures a place to wait out the cold. Shepherd’s guidance: remove leaves from anywhere they’re a slip hazard or blocking a drain, but keep them on flower borders, along the base of a hedge, or tucked into a back corner. A rake or broom does the job without the disturbance a leaf blower causes.

Think twice before cutting everything back

Pruning everything to the ground in fall can cost wild bees their winter home. “Avoiding the typical fall cleanup on plants and keeping stems of perennials and annuals creates nesting opportunities for tunnel-nesting bees such as small carpenter bees and leafcutters,” Shepherd says. The birds appreciate it too; they’ll forage on the seedheads through winter.

If a tidy front yard matters to you, Droege has a workable compromise: cut back to about a foot tall instead of to the ground. “A plant needs to be damaged or dead for bees to be able to use it,” he says, so a shorter cut still creates usable nesting structure without looking neglected.

If you’re already mid-cleanup, don’t compost what you’ve cut. “If any bees are already nesting in the stems, composting them will cause the end of that cycle,” Droege says. A loose pile left on the ground or behind the shed keeps the cycle going. Eierman adds that pithy stems from elderberry, raspberry, hydrangea, and Joe Pye weed are especially useful to cavity-nesting bees and can be bundled and left in place through winter.

Leave brush piles, snags, and cane fruit stems

Pruned branches can go into a brush pile rather than the compost. Loose piles don’t do much; Eierman notes they need to be “fairly tight and dense, providing cavities that shelter bees from rain.”

Dead or dying trees are candidates for keeping if they’re well away from the house. These are called snags. They develop hollow passages over time as beetles tunnel through the dead wood, and cavity-nesting bees use those passages the following season. A snag that’s too tall to feel comfortable about can be cut back to a manageable height without losing what makes it useful.

For cane fruits like raspberries, blackberries, and boysenberries, Droege says the same logic applies. “Cane fruits only fruit in year two,” he says. “Instead of cutting them to the ground, trimming them to a foot tall provides the best nesting material for a whole series of native wild bees.”

Leave bare patches of soil undisturbed

Most native bees nest in the ground and need bare, uncompacted soil to excavate their nests. “Don’t try to repair all the bare ground — leave the open areas, as bees like to nest there,” says Droege. Sandy or loamy soil in a sunny spot is ideal, but even a few square feet counts. If a bare patch feels too sparse, Eierman says planting very sparsely may still leave enough exposed soil between plants; just skip the mulch or landscape fabric, as both block bees from getting in. Treat it as wild habitat rather than an incomplete garden bed: no tilling, no cleaning up, not even in spring.

Keep some flowers going through fall

Most bees have wrapped up their nesting cycle by the time temperatures drop, but sweat bees and mining bees are still out foraging late in the season. Goldenrod and asters are the flowers they’re looking for. Having something in bloom through fall, and building toward a range of bloom times from spring through the end of the season, gives different species something to work with at different points in the year. “Expanding your garden for next spring and reducing your lawn is the biggest thing you can do for wild bees,” Droege says.

Eierman says it best: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Leave the leaves. Don’t compost the stems. Keep a corner wild. That’s most of it.

articles.personality_title: How simple fall garden care helps native bees survive winter
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every autumn, gardeners often clean up their yards by cutting plants, raking leaves, and clearing garden beds. This makes the garden look neat for spring but can harm native wild bees that live and nest there.

**What happened** – Experts from the Xerces Society and USGS explain that many wild bees spend winter in nests hidden in leaf piles, hollow stems, and bare soil in gardens. Instead of removing these natural shelters, gardeners are encouraged to leave leaves in safe spots, avoid cutting plants all the way down, keep brush piles and dead wood, and leave some bare soil undisturbed. These simple steps help bees survive the cold months.

**Impact** – This advice supports over 3,600 native bee species in the U.S., many of which are in decline. By changing how we clean gardens in fall, we provide safe places for solitary bees to hatch next year. This helps protect important pollinators that plants and gardens rely on.

**What's next step** – Gardeners can start by leaving leaves on flower borders, trimming plants only partially, saving stems and brush piles, and keeping bare soil spots. Over time, more gardens will become safe habitats for wild bees, helping their populations recover.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Leaving leaves, stems, and bare soil in your garden this fall gives native wild bees a better chance to survive winter and thrive next year.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment prendre soin de son jardin en automne pour aider les abeilles sauvages à passer l’hiver
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque automne, les jardiniers nettoient souvent leur jardin en coupant les plantes, en ramassant les feuilles et en dégageant les plates-bandes. Cela rend le jardin propre pour le printemps, mais peut nuire aux abeilles sauvages qui y nichent.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des experts du Xerces Society et de l’USGS expliquent que beaucoup d’abeilles sauvages passent l’hiver dans des nids cachés dans les tas de feuilles, les tiges creuses et le sol nu du jardin. Au lieu de tout enlever, ils conseillent de laisser les feuilles dans des endroits sûrs, de ne pas couper les plantes jusqu’au sol, de conserver les tas de branches mortes et de laisser le sol nu tranquille. Ces gestes simples aident les abeilles à survivre au froid.

**Impact** – Ce conseil aide plus de 3 600 espèces d’abeilles sauvages aux États-Unis, dont beaucoup sont en déclin. En changeant nos façons de nettoyer le jardin en automne, on offre un refuge sûr aux abeilles solitaires pour qu’elles émergent au printemps. Cela protège des pollinisateurs essentiels pour les plantes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les jardiniers peuvent commencer par laisser les feuilles sur les bordures de fleurs, tailler les plantes partiellement, garder les tiges et tas de branches, et préserver les zones de sol nu. Avec le temps, plus de jardins deviendront des habitats sûrs pour les abeilles sauvages.

**Résumé en une phrase** – En laissant feuilles, tiges et sol nu dans votre jardin cet automne, vous aidez les abeilles sauvages à mieux passer l’hiver et à prospérer au printemps.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo cuidar tu jardín en otoño para ayudar a las abejas silvestres a sobrevivir el invierno
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada otoño, los jardineros suelen limpiar sus jardines cortando plantas, recogiendo hojas y despejando las camas. Esto hace que el jardín se vea ordenado para la primavera, pero puede dañar a las abejas silvestres que anidan allí.

**Qué pasó** – Expertos del Xerces Society y del USGS explican que muchas abejas silvestres pasan el invierno en nidos escondidos en montones de hojas, tallos huecos y suelo descubierto en los jardines. En lugar de quitar todo, aconsejan dejar las hojas en lugares seguros, no cortar las plantas hasta el suelo, conservar los montones de ramas y dejar el suelo descubierto sin tocar. Estos pasos simples ayudan a las abejas a sobrevivir el frío.

**Impacto** – Este consejo apoya a más de 3,600 especies nativas de abejas en Estados Unidos, muchas en declive. Cambiando cómo limpiamos los jardines en otoño, damos refugio seguro a las abejas solitarias para que salgan en primavera. Esto protege polinizadores importantes para las plantas.

**Próximo paso** – Los jardineros pueden empezar por dejar las hojas en los bordes de flores, podar las plantas parcialmente, conservar tallos y montones de ramas, y mantener áreas de suelo descubierto. Con el tiempo, más jardines serán hábitats seguros para las abejas silvestres.

**Resumen en una frase** – Dejar hojas, tallos y suelo descubierto en tu jardín este otoño ayuda a las abejas silvestres a sobrevivir el invierno y prosperar en primavera.
